A reader’s guide

Understand a property record

A deed amount can differ from the price of a home. A missing mortgage match can leave financing unknown. Here is what to check in the documents.

One transfer can have several amounts

The deed’s consideration clause, the transfer-tax form’s full sale price and the registry’s indexed amount are separate fields. Read each in context and keep a separate transcription. A nominal amount in the deed does not settle the price question.

Illustrative example · not an actual transaction

Deed consideration
$10The operative clause may use a nominal sum and refer to other consideration. Check the rest of the instrument.
Full sale price on the tax form
$750,000This is the amount the form calls the full sale price. Check its parcel count and the nature of the conveyance.
ACRIS indexed amount
$750,000An indexed field helps find the document. It does not replace reading the deed or establish an arm’s-length sale.

In a transfer covering several parcels, the form can give the total consideration for the bundle. Assigning the full amount to every parcel would count the same price more than once.

What to check before using the record

Identify the instrument

Read its title and operative clause. An ordinary deed, a referee’s deed and a deed in lieu can describe different kinds of transfer. A lender taking title need not be a purchase at a negotiated market price.

Match the parcel

The borough, block and lot identify a tax parcel. A condominium sale may be listed under a billing lot while the deed identifies a unit lot. Check all parcels and any property schedule.

Separate the dates

A document’s execution date and its recording date can differ. A nearby date makes a mortgage a candidate for review; timing alone does not prove it financed the purchase.

Read the parties’ roles

Match the buyer with the borrower and the property with the collateral. Read the mortgage’s purpose and related instruments. Seller financing can count as purchase financing; a refinance or agreement modifying an old loan may not.

A mortgage search has limits

Imagine a $750,000 sale and a $500,000 mortgage recorded nearby on the same parcel. Those facts justify opening the mortgage. A firm purchase-financing call also needs the borrower, collateral and instrument terms to fit. A cover page can leave that question unresolved.

A failed search means no qualifying match was found under the search rules. It can miss a differently dated instrument, another parcel in a bundle, or a condominium unit that was not linked. It does not establish an unfinanced purchase.

Coverage asks how many eligible records were linked. Agreement asks whether two methods give the same answer. Accuracy requires comparison with a sufficiently reliable reference. High coverage or agreement does not by itself establish accuracy.

Keep a record of what you read

Save the document ID and URL, viewer and document page numbers, each amount and its field name, the parcel list, relevant dates and the clause supporting your interpretation. Record unreadable pages and contrary evidence. If the documents do not settle the question, record what remains unknown.
